Fundamentals

What is a Memristor?

A memristor is the fourth fundamental circuit element — alongside resistors, capacitors, and inductors — first theorized by Leon Chua in 1971 and physically realized in 2008.

Memory + Resistor = Memristor. Its resistance depends on the history of current that has flowed through it — like a resistor with memory.
Neuromorphic computing: memristors mimic synapses, enabling brain-like computation at a fraction of the energy cost.
Key property: When power is removed, the memristor remembers its last resistance state. Non-volatile, analog memory built in.
The four fundamental circuit elements

The Problem

Why Are Memristors Hard?

Despite their promise, conventional memristors face three critical barriers to widespread adoption.

💸

Cost

Rare-earth materials and cleanroom fabrication make conventional memristors prohibitively expensive to manufacture at scale.

⚡

Volatility

Many implementations degrade quickly under radiation or environmental stress, limiting deployment in aerospace and harsh conditions.

📉

Inconsistency

Cycle-to-cycle variability in resistance states makes precise analog computation unreliable without expensive error correction.

The Solution

Enter the Mushroom

Mushrooms directly solve the problems with conventional memristor production — and open doors to biological tech applications impossible with silicon.

🌱

Abundant & fast-growing. Cultivated in days from agricultural waste. Zero cleanroom or rare-earth materials needed.

♻️

Fully biodegradable. Unlike silicon chips, myco-memristors are compostable at end-of-life.

☢️

Radiation-resistant. Fungal structures are resilient to radiation — viable candidates for aerospace applications.

🧠

Self-healing & neuromorphic. Mycelium naturally exhibits adaptive electrical signaling akin to neuronal spiking.

💰

Extremely inexpensive. Growing blocks cost ~$20. No specialized equipment for cultivation.

Prior Work

Existing Research

PLOS One · 2025
Sustainable memristors from shiitake mycelium for high-frequency bioelectronics

Researchers at Ohio State University grew shiitake mushroom mycelium into highly accurate memristors. Their memristors demonstrated stable operation for 2+ months and 1,000 reads/writes. Additionally, they held all the benefits anticipated by using the mushrooms: low-power, radiation-resistant, self-healing, neuromorphic.

Methodology

Experimental Setup

Our lab setup — oscilloscope, breadboard circuit, and mycelium petri dishes
1
Grow mycelium samples
9 petri dishes inoculated with Lentinula edodes (shiitake) spawn on grain substrate. Dishes sealed with parafilm and incubated at room temperature until the mycelium fully colonized the substrate — visible as a white, fluffy network spreading across the surface.
2
Dry the mycelium disk
Once fully colonized, dishes were opened and left to dry at room temperature. The mycelium consolidates into a rigid, paper-like disk. Two wire electrodes were then inserted directly into the disk at fixed spacing to make electrical contact with the mycelium network.
3
Apply signal & measure
A sine wave was applied across the mycelium disk via a function generator. Current was inferred by measuring voltage across a 1 MΩ sense resistor in series. Both an oscilloscope and Arduino (analog pin A1) captured voltage and current simultaneously for cross-validation.
4
Plot IV curves
Captured voltage and current data were plotted as IV curves. We looked specifically for a pinched hysteresis loop passing through the origin — the defining signature of memristive behavior — across multiple samples and frequency settings.
Two of our 9 mycelium samples
Circuit Design
Circuit used to obtain IV curves — sine input, mycelium as DUT, 1 MΩ sense resistor

A sine wave is applied across the mycelium. The voltage across a known 1 MΩ resistor in series gives the current. Plotting input voltage vs. measured current reveals the IV characteristic — and any memristive hysteresis loop.

Both an oscilloscope and an Arduino (analog read on pin A1) capture the output simultaneously for cross-validation.

Applications

What Could We Build?

If a working myco-memristor can be reliably produced, it opens the door to circuits that have historically required rare-earth materials and precision fabrication — achieved instead with a petri dish.

Leon Chua · 1971

The Sustained Chaos Circuit

Leon Chua theorized and built the first non-passive memristor. With it, he created a sustained chaos circuit that outputs voltages varying by up to 3V — producing controlled, chaotic oscillations with no external forcing. The memristor used a combination of two op-amps and resistor networks to achieve memristance, but would "forget" its values when powered off.

Chua's chaos circuit — 18mH inductor, 100nF & 10nF caps, 1.8kΩ resistor
Theoretical ReRAM circuit — 500kHz input, crossbar array
HP Labs · 2007

Resistive RAM (ReRAM)

In 2007, HP Labs fabricated the first passive memristor. As transistor circuits approached a physical size limit, memristors were hyped as the next leap in memory — Resistive RAM (ReRAM). Unlike flash memory, ReRAM switches resistance states using tiny voltage pulses, consuming far less power.

With a working myco-memristor, we could replicate the ReRAM crossbar array shown here — storing values in the resistance state of each mycelium junction, erasing and rewriting them with voltage pulses. Biological, compostable, non-volatile memory.

Findings

Results

Honest Assessment

Our Mushristors Are Not True Memristors

Our myco-memristors hold capacitance and resistance — but they are not true memristors. This isn't a failure unique to us: real-world memristors broadly fail to conform to Chua's original mathematical definition (M(q) = dφ/dq). They only retain resistance states imperfectly. "True" passive memristors have technically existed for years — so why do we still use DRAM and SRAM?

Problem 1 — Cost

Components are expensive to fabricate. A memristor-based memory cell requires ~30 transistors and several capacitors — a significant jump in complexity over DRAM.

Problem 2 — Inconsistency

The mathematics simply don't hold up consistently the way Ohm's Law (V=IR) or capacitor charge (Q=CV) do. This fundamental inconsistency has prevented practical realization — and our study reaffirms this conclusion.

What Our Mushristors Actually Are

Memory-dependent impedance — hydrated mushristors behave like a memory-dependent impedance element that is neither a pure resistor nor a pure capacitor.

Frequency-dependent capacitance — they can be modeled as having an effective capacitance that depends most heavily on the input frequency.

Resistive but hard to characterize — mushristors are also resistive, but this component is more difficult to isolate and quantify consistently.

Analog short-term memory — they exhibit some short-term memory of past electrical states, analogous to biological synaptic behavior, though this fades rather than persisting non-volatilely.

Our Measurements

Myco-Memristor IV Curves

Our oscilloscope IV plots across three samples — blue Lissajous curves

Signal Parameters

Best results obtained using a low-voltage ~0.8V–1V square wave at 1–2 Hz, consistent with the methodology of the Ohio State paper. Lower frequencies allowed the mycelium's slow ionic response to register clearly.

Resistance Measurements

Resistance across any path of the mushristor measured at ~80–90 kΩ for slightly hydrated mushrooms. Fully dried mushrooms reached as high as 9 MΩ — making them excellent for high-gain op-amp circuits where large resistances are needed.

Key Finding — Curve Comparison
RC circuit IV plot — nearly identical shape to our mushristor curves

Our resulting curves look strikingly similar to a standard RC circuit IV plot, not the pinched hysteresis loop of a true memristor. The mushristor holds both capacitance and resistance — but not the memristive switching behavior.

This confirms that a true passive memristor — one that retains state without power, unlike Chua's op-amp implementation — remains out of reach. Our mushrooms exhibit memristor-adjacent behavior, but the underlying physics aligns more closely with a leaky capacitor than a memory resistor.

Waveform Comparison

Target vs. Test Behavior

Left: Target memristor behavior  ·  Right: Our mushristor test results  ·  Purple = input · Yellow = mushroom response · Orange = difference

Insufficient Capacitance

The mushroom tissue lacks sufficient capacitance to produce the hysteresis behavior of a true memristor. The stored charge dissipates too quickly to sustain the resistance state between switching events.

Square Wave Response

In the square wave test, the device charges slowly and cannot sustain the input voltage — causing the signal to fall off as voltage rises. The mushristor behaves almost like a low-pass filter, rounding the sharp edges of the square wave.

Triangle Wave Response

The triangle wave result is more consistent with predicted memristor output. The gradual ramp allows the tissue to track the signal more faithfully — suggesting that slow, ramp-type inputs better match the mushristor's ionic response speed.

Hydration Effects

Impact of Hydration

When dehydrated, mushristors lose most of their capacitance and begin to behave purely as resistors. The complex impedance collapses — what was a frequency-dependent, memory-adjacent element becomes a simple ohmic device.

The straight-line IV curve on the right matches the ideal resistor characteristic on the left almost exactly — confirming that moisture is the critical variable enabling any memristive-adjacent behavior. Without hydration, there is no capacitance, no memory, and no interesting dynamics.

Left: ideal resistor (R = V/I)  ·  Right: our dehydrated mushristor — a near-perfect straight line

When the mycelium disk is fully dehydrated, the mushristor loses nearly all of its capacitive character. The IV curve collapses to a straight line — indistinguishable from a plain ohmic resistor obeying V = IR.

False Positives

A Couple of False Positives

We ran into a couple of false positive situations that seemed like memristive behavior. One happened because we were working on a metal surface that was inducing capacitance into the circuit. The second instance was trickier — when we touched the circuit while it was running, it also induced capacitance that momentarily seemed like memristive behavior.

Oscilloscope curves that appeared to show memristive hysteresis — both were capacitive artifacts
Possible Circuits

Mycomemristors in the Wild

Despite not being true passive memristors, our mushristors are still viable circuit components. Here's a working example that proves it.

Circuit Schematic

40 Hz sine wave input · 10kΩ gain resistor · mushristor as Rf

Dried Mycelium Disk with Electrode Wires
Circuit Demo

Amplified output through speaker — audible proof of circuit function

Amplifying Memristor Circuit

This circuit uses a non-inverting amplifier configuration, with the mushristor placed where Rf would normally go. Low 1V sine waves at varying frequencies were fed in as Vin, amplified by the op-amp stage, and sent through a speaker. Without this circuit the signal isn't audible — with it, it is.

🍄

Mycomemristors are viable for circuits. Even as a leaky capacitor rather than a true memristor, our mushristor functions meaningfully as a feedback element — demonstrating real-world utility for bio-based circuit components.
